title: StarGAN: Unified Generative Adversarial Networks for Multi-Domain Image-to-Image Translation
authors: Yunjey Choi, Minje Choi, Munyoung Kim, Jung-Woo Ha, Sunghun Kim, Jaegul Choo

pages.title: One Model for Many Translations
pages.subtitle: Replacing a zoo of generators with a single network

blocks.html: Image-to-image translation (e.g. changing hair color, age, or expression) had a painful limitation. To translate between $k$ domains, prior methods needed a separate generator for nearly every pair, which scales as roughly $k(k-1)$ models. Training and storing all of them is wasteful, and each model only sees data from its own two domains.
We propose StarGAN, a novel and scalable approach that can perform image-to-image translations for multiple domains using only a single model.

Use one generator that also takes a target domain label as input, telling it which translation to perform. Because the single generator learns from all domains at once, it shares knowledge across them and can even handle multiple datasets together.

pages.title: A Label-Conditioned Generator
pages.subtitle: The target domain is just another input

blocks.html: The generator $G$ takes an input image $x$ and a target domain label $c$ (for example, "blond hair" or "smiling"), and produces a translated image $G(x, c)$. The label is fed in as extra channels appended to the image. By randomly varying $c$ during training, one $G$ learns to map any image into any domain.

The discriminator $D$ does double duty. It judges whether an image is real or fake and predicts which domain it belongs to. The authors write this as $D : x \rightarrow \{ D_{src}(x), D_{cls}(x) \}$, a real/fake head and a domain-classification head sharing the same body.
Standard GAN pressure makes translated images look real. $G$ tries to fool $D_{src}$ while $D$ tries to tell real from generated:

Realism alone does not guarantee the output lands in the requested domain. So $D$ learns to classify real images into their true domains, and $G$ is rewarded when its outputs are classified as the target domain $c$:

Reading it plainly: $\mathcal{L}_{cls}^{r}$ trains $D$ to recognize the original domain $c'$ of real images; $\mathcal{L}_{cls}^{f}$ pushes $G$ to make images the classifier reads as the target domain $c$.

Nothing so far stops $G$ from changing more than necessary. To force it to preserve content (identity, background) and only edit the targeted attribute, StarGAN borrows cycle consistency: translating to $c$ and back to the original domain $c'$ should recover the input:

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{rec} = \mathbb{E}_{x, c, c'}\big[ \big\| x - G(G(x, c), c') \big\|_1 \big]

blocks.html: The same single generator is reused for both the forward and backward translation, which is what keeps the model count at one.
Combining the pieces, with weights $\lambda_{cls}$ and $\lambda_{rec}$:
The authors use $\lambda_{cls} = 1$ and $\lambda_{rec} = 10$, emphasizing content preservation, and use a Wasserstein-GAN gradient-penalty form of the adversarial term for stable training.

pages.title: The Mask Vector Trick
pages.subtitle: Training on datasets with different label sets

blocks.html: A subtle problem: different datasets label different things. CelebA has hair color and gender; RaFD has facial expressions. An image from one dataset has no labels for the other's attributes. Training naively would corrupt the unknown labels.

StarGAN solves this with a mask vector that tells the model which dataset a sample comes from, so the generator ignores the unspecified labels for that sample. This lets a single StarGAN jointly learn attributes from multiple datasets and even combine them, e.g. change hair color (CelebA) and expression (RaFD) on the same face.

pages.title: Why One Model Wins
pages.subtitle: Sharing data across domains pays off

blocks.html: In user studies on facial attribute transfer, StarGAN's outputs were strongly preferred over pair-wise baselines like DIAT, CycleGAN, and IcGAN, especially for multi-attribute edits. Because the single generator sees every domain, it learns shared facial structure once instead of relearning it per pair.

items: One generator and one discriminator handle all domains, instead of O(k^2) models.
Joint training across domains acts as data augmentation, improving image quality.
Multiple datasets can be combined via the mask vector for richer, composable edits.
